blogs.title: From ‘We Need to Come Inside’ to ‘Okay’: Voluntariness, Coercion, and Consent at the Door
blogs.description: Analyzes the Seventh Circuit’s treatment of voluntariness where an officer expressed, “we almost need to come inside,” and the occupant replied “Okay.” Explores how the panel reconciles that phrasing with Bumper’s prohibition on consent-by-claim-of-authority, the totality-of-the-circumstances framework from Schneckloth, and why clear-error review plus bodycam footage made the defendant’s coercion argument a hard sell.

blogs.title: After Caniglia: Consent Becomes the Workhorse for In-Home Welfare Checks
blogs.description: Situates the decision in post-Caniglia v. Strom doctrine limiting ‘community caretaking’ in the home, and explains why the court’s choice to rest exclusively on consent—eschewing exigent circumstances—reflects a broader trend. Assesses incentives for police to structure encounters as consensual welfare checks and the doctrinal risks if ‘need’ language becomes a standard script.

blogs.title: What Does ‘Okay’ Authorize? The Scope of Consent When Officers Enter to Check on Children
blogs.description: Examines the court’s application of Jimeno’s objective-reasonableness test to uphold a room-to-room scan to locate occupants and ensure safety. Considers how far consent to ‘check on the kids’ extends—locating a potentially dangerous adult, brief questioning, and a protective pat-down—and offers guidance on how occupants and officers can clarify or cabin scope in real time.

blogs.title: The Doctrines That Didn’t Decide the Case: Exigency and Inevitable Discovery Left Unaddressed
blogs.description: Explores the panel’s choice not to reach exigent circumstances or inevitable discovery, and what that omission signals about the preferred analytic path in domestic-violence 911 responses. Compares likely outcomes under Brigham City and similar exigency precedents, and flags how a different factual nuance (e.g., non-consent or visible injury) might force courts back to exigency analysis.

blogs.title: Bodycams, Scott v. Harris, and the New Appellate Deference in Suppression Litigation
blogs.description: Discusses the opinion’s reliance on body-worn camera footage to ‘evaporate’ factual disputes, tightening clear-error review of voluntariness and scope. Evaluates how video evidence reshapes suppression hearings, the framing of consent exchanges, and defense strategies for developing testimonial context that video may not capture (tone, off-camera cues, linguistic ambiguity).

blogs.title: Co-Occupant Consent in the Shadow of Randolph and Fernandez
blogs.description: Situates the ruling within the third-party consent line—Matlock, Georgia v. Randolph, and Fernandez v. California—highlighting why the absence of a contemporaneous objection by the suspect matters. Explores counterfactuals: how the analysis might shift if the non-consenting co-occupant appeared at the threshold, or if police re-solicited consent after locating him inside.

blogs.title: Practical Takeaways: Phrasing, Proof, and Preserving the Record in Consent Cases
blogs.description: Offers practitioner guidance. For officers: phrasing requests without implying authority, documenting explicit assent, and clarifying scope. For defense counsel: challenging ‘need’ language, eliciting testimony about hesitation or implied coercion, and using Randolph/Fernandez principles to frame objection timing. For judges: crafting findings that reckon with both video and subtle coercion cues.
